label: Proposition 141
t: Ban taxes and tracking based on miles driven
what: Amends the Arizona Constitution to bar the state and local governments from imposing any tax or fee based on miles a person drives, and from monitoring or limiting miles driven without the person's consent. Interstate commercial vehicles under fuel-tax/registration agreements and government-owned vehicles are exempt. Arizona has no mileage tax today.
y: A mileage-based tax or fee, and tracking of miles driven without consent, would be constitutionally prohibited.
n: The constitution stays as is; the Legislature or local governments could still consider a mileage-based fee in the future.
fiscal: No official fiscal estimate; Arizona currently levies no mileage tax, so there is no immediate change in revenue. Road funding relies on the 18-cent-per-gallon gas tax.
pro: Arizona Free Enterprise Club, Arizona Trucking Association, National Motorists Association, legislative Republicans
con: Southern Arizona Leadership Council, Civic Engagement Beyond Voting, legislative Democrats

reasons.transit: Permanently rules out a mileage-based fee as a future way to fund roads, leaving fuel taxes and other sources.

label: Proposition 142
t: Expand ban on race-based preferences and DEI
what: Expands Arizona's 2010 constitutional ban on preferential treatment (Prop 107). It bars requiring applicants, students, employees or contractors to support race-based diversity, equity and inclusion statements, bars public money for public-education offices that promote race-based preferential treatment, and bars race-based differences in discipline, with exceptions for health services, legal requirements and other reasons.
y: The constitution would specifically prohibit these DEI-related requirements, offices and practices in state and local government and public education.
n: The existing constitutional ban on preferential treatment stays as it is, without these added details.
pro: House Speaker Steve Montenegro (sponsor), Goldwater Institute, legislative Republicans
con: Legislative Democrats, Civic Engagement Beyond Voting

label: Proposition 144
t: Voter ID for all ballots incl. mail; election rules
what: Requires every voter, including mail voters, to show government-issued ID in each election, with the Legislature setting how mail voters do so. It also lets voters have ballots tabulated at their voting location on Election Day, bans foreign-national election spending, reaffirms that only citizens may vote, and sets a 'rationally connected to a legitimate state interest' standard for courts reviewing election laws (including early and mail voting). Applies to elections from Jan 1, 2028.
y: These ID, tabulation, campaign-finance and judicial-review rules would be added to the Arizona Constitution, and the Legislature must fund them.
n: Current election provisions stay; ID is required in person, and mail ballots continue to be verified by signature.
fiscal: No official dollar estimate; the measure requires the Legislature to appropriate whatever money is needed to implement it.
con: Former AZ Democratic Party chair Raquel Terán, former Phoenix Mayor Paul Johnson (No Labels Party chair), Civic Engagement Beyond Voting

label: Proposition 316
t: Cap city grocery taxes at 2%, require voter OK
what: Bars cities and towns from adopting or raising a tax on groceries (food for home consumption) between July 1, 2025 and June 30, 2027. After that, any new or higher grocery tax needs voter approval and cannot exceed 2%; cities already at 2% or more can keep their current rate but can never raise it. Existing rates are not cut.
y: City grocery taxes are frozen through mid-2027, then can rise only with voter approval and never above 2%.
n: Cities and towns keep their current authority to set grocery tax rates.
fiscal: No fiscal note on the final version. JLBC reported 70 of 91 cities/towns taxed groceries in FY2024, collecting $196.4M; the original full-repeal version was estimated to cost cities $227.6M a year from FY2028. The final version freezes rather than cuts rates, so the effect is on future increases only. No state General Fund impact.
con: Rural and small-city officials (e.g., Bisbee, Page, Taylor), Civic Engagement Beyond Voting

reasons.services: Limits future growth in a city revenue source worth about $196M a year statewide, which some smaller cities rely on for local services.

label: Proposition 317
what: Declares drug cartels (groups engaged in human smuggling, drug trafficking or acts of terrorism under Arizona law) to be terrorist organizations. Directs the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to use all lawful means within its authority to address threats from cartels, and states the measure does not support any asylum claim.
y: State law would label drug cartels terrorist organizations and direct state Homeland Security to address them.
n: Current terrorism and homeland-security laws stay as they are.
pro: House Speaker Steve Montenegro (sponsor), legislative Republicans
con: Arizonans for Freedom, Civic Engagement Beyond Voting; Brennan Center has raised concerns

label: Proposition 318
t: Sex-at-birth rules for school sports and locker rooms
what: The 'Protect Girls' Sports in Arizona Act' extends the existing public-school rule to private schools and athletic associations: teams must be designated male, female or coed by sex recorded at birth, and males may not join female teams. It bars schools and athletic associations from letting anyone use athletic restrooms, locker rooms or showers not designated for their sex at birth, and lets athletes sue entities that knowingly violate it.
y: These sports-team and private-space rules would apply to public and private schools and athletic associations, enforceable by lawsuits.
n: Current law stays, which applies the sports-team rule only to public schools and those competing against them.
pro: Protect Girls Sports in Arizona campaign, legislative Republicans
con: Progress Arizona, LGBTQ advocacy groups, Civic Engagement Beyond Voting

label: Proposition 319
t: Restrict traffic cameras; voter approval to keep them
what: Bars state agencies and local governments from using photo enforcement (speed and red-light cameras) unless they have a contract in place by Dec 31, 2026. Local governments with existing systems must win voter approval at the next general election to keep them, and again every 10 years; if voters say no, the cameras must stop within 90 days.
y: No new traffic-camera programs; existing local programs continue only with periodic voter approval.
n: State and local governments keep their current authority to use photo enforcement.
con: League of Arizona Cities and Towns, law-enforcement agencies, Civic Engagement Beyond Voting

label: Proposition 320
t: Require large school districts to spend 60% on instruction
what: Requires school districts with at least 7,500 students, or operating in a county of 500,000+ people (Maricopa, Pima, Pinal), to spend at least 60% of operational spending on direct instruction as defined by the Auditor General. Starting in 2027-28, districts below 60% must raise that share by at least 0.5 percentage point a year. Non-compliant districts lose 25% of their Classroom Site Fund allocation per year of non-compliance (up to 100% after four years), unless the Superintendent grants a waiver; withheld money goes to compliant districts.
y: Covered districts must move spending toward direct instruction or face cuts to their Classroom Site Fund money.
n: School districts keep current budgeting rules.
fiscal: No official fiscal estimate. Reporting cites statewide instructional spending at about 52% of budgets; withheld Classroom Site Fund money is redistributed to compliant districts rather than saved.
con: Save Our Schools Arizona, Civic Engagement Beyond Voting
